description: Composite figure of two 3D finite-element shell-model contour maps of the body-in-white (BIW) of a Golf V (Volkswagen), in which every sheet part is coloured by its required shell thickness in millimetres. (a) shows the BIW with HSLA steels; its vertical colour bar is labelled 0.750, 1.125, 1.500, 1.875, 2.250, 2.625 and 3.000 mm in seven swatches ordered white, blue, cyan, green, yellow, red, magenta. (b) shows the same BIW built from a low-density ferrite-based duplex steel; its colour bar is labelled 0.600, 1.167, 1.733, 2.300, 2.867, 3.433 and 4.000 mm with the identical swatch order, and the axis title "Shell thickness (mm)" is printed beneath it. The colour distributions differ markedly: panel (a) is dominated by green, cyan and yellow parts (the middle classes of its scale), whereas in panel (b) the great majority of parts are dark blue or light blue, the lowest classes of its own scale. Read together, the two panels demonstrate that replacing HSLA steel sheets by the low-density steel shifts the required shell thickness to lower values throughout the same BIW geometry, the change being attributed to the lower Young's modulus of the low-density steel.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is a 3D colour-contour map of a car body-in-white in which each sheet part is coloured by shell thickness; its colour bar is labelled 0.750, 1.125, 1.500, 1.875, 2.250, 2.625 and 3.000 mm.
Panel (b) shows the same BIW model with a colour bar labelled 0.600, 1.167, 1.733, 2.300, 2.867, 3.433 and 4.000 mm, i.e. a different (extended) thickness scale from panel (a).
Both colour bars use the same seven-swatch order — white, blue, cyan, green, yellow, red, magenta — running from the lowest to the highest thickness class.
The label 'Shell thickness (mm)' is printed beneath the colour bar of panel (b).

In (a) most parts are coloured green, cyan and yellow (middle classes of the 0.750-3.000 mm scale), whereas in (b) the majority of parts are dark blue or light blue, the two lowest classes of the 0.600-4.000 mm scale.

The caption identifies (a) as shell thickness with HSLA steels and (b) as shell thickness with the low-density steel, in an engineering study for replacing HSLA steels in the BIW of a Golf V, Volkswagen by a ferrite-based duplex steel.
The caption states that the shift of shell thickness to lower values was predicted to result in 14.5% weight saving in the BIW; the value 14.5% is not printed anywhere in either panel.

The citing text states that torsional stiffness, the ratio of applied torsion moment to angle of twist, was kept constant for the whole BIW after replacing HSLA steel sheets by low-density steel sheets.
The citing text attributes the required change in sheet thickness to the lower Young's modulus of the low-density steel.

The citing text states that a weight reduction of 14.5% of the BIW was predicted for replacing all HSLA steel sheets by the low-density steel sheets, while noting that considerations other than torsional stiffness would also influence part gauges.

subfigures.description: 3D colour-contour map (FE shell model) of a car body-in-white in which each part is coloured by shell thickness; the legend reads 0.750, 1.125, 1.500, 1.875, 2.250, 2.625 and 3.000 mm with white, blue, cyan, green, yellow, red and magenta swatches. Most parts are green, cyan or yellow, with scattered red and dark-blue regions.

The same 3D BIW shell model, now for the low-density ferrite-based duplex steel; the legend reads 0.600, 1.167, 1.733, 2.300, 2.867, 3.433 and 4.000 mm with the same swatch order, and the caption 'Shell thickness (mm)' is printed at the bottom right. The body is mostly dark blue and light blue (lowest classes), with a few green, yellow and magenta parts.

unreadable_items: No numeric thickness value is printed on any individual BIW part; only the colour-bar class boundaries are legible, so per-part thicknesses can only be assigned to a class, not to a number.
